title: Microsoft SC-200 Security Operations Analyst
summary: Microsoft SC-200 Security Operations Analyst is an associate-level certification that validates the ability to detect, investigate and respond to threats using Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Defender for Cloud and Microsoft Sentinel. It is aimed at security analysts who already work in a security operations centre or are moving into one, and it assumes working familiarity with Windows and Linux fundamentals, networking, and at least some Microsoft 365 and Azure administration. For an employer the credential is evidence that a candidate can read a KQL result set, pivot from an alert to an affected entity, contain a compromised device or mailbox, and carry a Sentinel incident from triage to closure instead of escalating everything upward. The exam is proctored and scenario driven, mixing multiple choice, drag-and-drop, case-study and interactive portal-style items, with results reported as a scaled score that requires 700 on a 1000-point scale to pass; questions are phrased around concrete analyst actions, so portal fluency matters as much as recall. Hands-on practice changes the outcome far more than reading does. Analysts who build analytics rules, tune noisy detections, run advanced hunting queries, connect data sources and rehearse playbook-driven response in a tenant of their own recognise the distractors immediately, because the wrong answers usually describe actions that read well in documentation but fail operationally. Reading alone tends to produce shallow recall of feature names, which is precisely what the case-study items are designed to expose.
objectives: Defender XDR fundamentals: Explain how signals from Defender for Endpoint, Defender for Office 365, Defender for Identity and Defender for Cloud Apps are correlated into a unified alert and incident model.
Threat investigation in Defender XDR: Use advanced hunting queries, alert triage views, entity and evidence panes, and automated investigation to establish scope, root cause and blast radius.
Incident response actions: Apply containment and remediation actions such as device isolation, live response, mailbox remediation and app governance, and record the reasoning behind each decision.

Microsoft Defender for Cloud: Assess cloud security posture, interpret secure score recommendations, and prioritise misconfigurations and workload protection gaps across Azure and multicloud resources.

Sentinel data ingestion: Connect data sources with built-in connectors, codeless connectors and the Logs Ingestion API, then validate parsing and normalisation into the advanced security information model.
Detection engineering: Author scheduled, near-real-time and fusion analytics rules in KQL, tune rule thresholds against false positives, and manage detection content in a version-controlled workflow.
Hunting and automation: Build hunting queries and workbooks for proactive threat hunting, and implement Logic Apps playbooks that automate triage and response steps consistently.
Incident management in Microsoft Sentinel: Triage, assign, collaborate on and close incidents, including entity mapping, task tracking and defensible evidence handling.

beginner.definition: SC-200 is a Microsoft exam for security analysts who work in a security operations centre (the team that watches for attacks all day). It tests whether you can read alerts, investigate what happened, and contain a real problem. It focuses on the everyday work of spotting and stopping threats rather than designing policy.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attacks do not announce themselves politely. They arrive as a flood of alerts, and most of them are false alarms. An analyst must find the few that matter before damage spreads. This exam proves you can do that calmly with real tools. Teams without this skill either miss real attacks or drown in noise.
howItWorks: A signal arrives. A tool notices something odd, such as a strange sign-in or a file behaving badly.
You read the alert and ask simple questions. Who did this, which machine, and when did it start?
You search the logs (the recorded history of activity) to see what else the same account or device did.
You decide how serious it is. A failed login matters less than a stolen password in active use.
You contain the problem. You may isolate a device or block an account so the attacker loses access.
You record what you did, close the case, and tune the alert so the next one is clearer.
beginner.example: Picture a busy hospital front desk at night. Patients arrive constantly, and most only need a plaster. A few are seriously ill and must be seen at once. The desk clerk cannot treat everyone, so they sort fast and move the urgent cases to a doctor. A security analyst works the same way with alerts. You sort quickly, check the worst first, and hand serious cases to the right team.
takeaways: Most alerts are noise, so your first job is to decide what deserves attention.
Containment is temporary. You stop the bleeding, then investigate properly.
Write down your reasoning while it is fresh, because others will read it later.
